articles.title: This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies.
articles.content:
A bird that migrates thousands of miles has revealed a surprising secret about how wings work. Scientists have discovered that European nightjars sacrifice flight efficiency for agility and use an unexpected wingbeat technique previously associated mainly with bats and insects.

The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nighttime hunter that makes an extraordinary annual migration between Europe and southern Africa. Yet the wings that carry it across vast distances must also perform a very different task: helping the bird catch insects while flying slowly and making sharp turns.

Scientists at Lund University have discovered that these competing demands come with a surprising trade-off. Although the nightjar is built to handle long migrations, its wings are not perfectly optimized for efficient flight at higher speeds.

Why Nightjar Wings Sacrifice Efficiency for Agility

To investigate how nightjars fly, researchers studied the birds in a wind tunnel, recording their movements at different speeds and measuring the patterns of airflow left behind their wings.

The experiments revealed that the nightjar's broad wing tips, which likely help it maneuver during slow flight, become a disadvantage as the bird flies faster. At higher speeds, its wings generate lift less efficiently. Lift is the aerodynamic force that helps keep a bird airborne.

The findings challenge the assumption that birds traveling enormous distances must have wings optimized primarily for efficient long-distance flight.

"This runs counter to the intuitive image of a long-distance migrant as a perfectly optimized flying machine. Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands. The bird can fly slowly and maneuver while hunting, but the trade-off is reduced efficiency in lift generation at higher speeds," says Christoffer Johansson, associate professor at Lund University.

Scientists Discover an Unexpected Wingbeat Trick

The researchers also uncovered another surprising feature of the nightjar's flight. Even as the bird raises its wings during the upward portion of each wingbeat, it continues to generate thrust, the force that helps propel it forward.

This is unusual because such an active upward wing movement, known as an upstroke, has previously been linked mainly to the flight mechanics of bats and insects rather than birds.

The discovery suggests that animals with very different evolutionary histories may have developed similar aerodynamic solutions to the challenges of flying.

"What's interesting is that the same type of aerodynamic solution seems to appear in quite different animals. This suggests that the upstroke does not have to be merely a passive or lift generating part of the wingbeat. It can be actively used to generate thrust when the wings cannot be folded very much," says Christoffer Johansson.

What Bird Flight Reveals About Evolution and Flying Robots

The results offer a broader lesson about how evolution shapes animals that depend on the same body structures for different activities.

Rather than producing wings perfectly suited to one purpose, evolution can favor designs that balance several competing needs. For the nightjar, that means combining the ability to migrate across continents with the agility required to hunt insects at low speeds.

Understanding these compromises could also lead to improvements in aviation technology, particularly drones and other robotic aircraft that use flapping wings.

Like birds, these machines may face mechanical restrictions on how much their wings can fold during each wingbeat. Learning how nightjars generate thrust during the upstroke could help engineers develop more effective ways to move through the air.

Researchers now hope to determine whether this unusual flight mechanism is widespread among other birds and flying animals or whether it represents a more specialized adaptation.

"We now want to investigate how common this way of generating force is among other birds and flying animals. It could help us understand which aerodynamic principles are specific to the nightjar and which are more general. This knowledge may also inspire the development of new types of flapping aircraft," Christoffer Johansson concludes.

articles.personality_title: European nightjar’s unique wing moves balance long flights and agile hunting
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The European nightjar is a bird that flies thousands of miles every year, migrating between Europe and southern Africa. It hunts insects at night, needing to fly slowly and turn quickly to catch its prey.

**What happened** – Scientists at Lund University studied how nightjars fly and found that their wings are not built just for fast, efficient flight. Instead, the wings are shaped to help the bird move quickly and easily when hunting, even if that makes long-distance flying less efficient. They also discovered that nightjars create thrust during the upward part of their wingbeat, a movement mostly seen in bats and insects before.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that the nightjar’s wings are a clever balance between flying far and hunting well. It challenges the idea that birds migrating long distances only have wings designed for speed and efficiency. The unusual thrust during the upward wingbeat could inspire new designs for drones and flying robots, helping them move better through the air.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to find out if other birds or flying animals use the same wing technique. Understanding this could tell us which flight features are unique to nightjars and which are common. This knowledge might help engineers create better flying machines that copy nature’s smart designs.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The European nightjar’s wings balance long-distance travel and precise hunting with a surprising wingbeat that could inspire future flying technology.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les ailes uniques de la nuitjar européenne allient longs voyages et chasse agile
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La nuitjar européenne est un oiseau qui parcourt des milliers de kilomètres chaque année, migrant entre l’Europe et l’Afrique australe. Il chasse les insectes la nuit, devant voler lentement et tourner rapidement pour attraper ses proies.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques de l’Université de Lund ont étudié le vol des nuitjars et ont découvert que leurs ailes ne sont pas conçues uniquement pour un vol rapide et efficace. Au contraire, leurs ailes sont faites pour aider l’oiseau à se déplacer rapidement et facilement lors de la chasse, même si cela rend le vol longue distance moins efficace. Ils ont aussi découvert que la nuitjar génère une poussée pendant la phase ascendante du battement d’ailes, un mouvement surtout observé chez les chauves-souris et les insectes.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que les ailes de la nuitjar sont un équilibre intelligent entre le vol sur de longues distances et la chasse précise. Elle remet en question l’idée que les oiseaux migrateurs ont des ailes uniquement adaptées à la vitesse et à l’efficacité. Cette poussée pendant le battement ascendant pourrait inspirer de nouveaux modèles pour les drones et les robots volants, améliorant leur déplacement dans l’air.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent savoir si d’autres oiseaux ou animaux volants utilisent cette même technique d’ailes. Comprendre cela pourrait révéler quelles caractéristiques de vol sont uniques aux nuitjars et lesquelles sont communes. Ces connaissances pourraient aider les ingénieurs à créer de meilleures machines volantes qui s’inspirent des solutions naturelles.

**Une phrase clé** – Les ailes de la nuitjar européenne équilibrent les longs voyages et la chasse précise grâce à un battement d’ailes surprenant qui pourrait inspirer la technologie du vol de demain.
articles.personality_title_es: Las alas únicas del chotacabras europeo combinan vuelos largos y caza ágil
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El chotacabras europeo es un ave que vuela miles de kilómetros cada año, migrando entre Europa y el sur de África. Caza insectos de noche, necesitando volar despacio y girar rápido para atraparlos.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos de la Universidad de Lund estudiaron cómo vuela el chotacabras y descubrieron que sus alas no están hechas solo para volar rápido y eficientemente. En cambio, las alas ayudan al ave a moverse con agilidad al cazar, aunque eso haga menos eficiente el vuelo de larga distancia. También encontraron que el chotacabras genera empuje durante la subida de las alas, un movimiento antes visto principalmente en murciélagos e insectos.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra que las alas del chotacabras son un equilibrio inteligente entre viajar lejos y cazar con precisión. Desafía la idea de que las aves migratorias tienen alas solo para velocidad y eficiencia. El empuje durante la subida del batir de alas podría inspirar nuevos diseños para drones y robots voladores, ayudándolos a moverse mejor en el aire.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren saber si otras aves o animales voladores usan la misma técnica de vuelo. Entender esto podría revelar qué características de vuelo son únicas del chotacabras y cuáles se repiten en otros. Este conocimiento podría ayudar a ingenieros a crear mejores máquinas voladoras que imiten soluciones naturales.

**Una frase clave** – Las alas del chotacabras europeo equilibran viajes largos y caza precisa con un batir de alas sorprendente que podría inspirar la tecnología de vuelo futura.
